messages.content: I'm building a Spring Boot backend for a SaaS product. I prefer Kotlin over Java because the null-safety model keeps me sane, and I always use Ktor for the internal service-to-service mesh.
Kotlin and Spring Boot are a great pairing. Kotlin's null-safety and coroutines work especially well alongside Ktor for the internal mesh. Here's a starter layout...
I live in Berlin, I work remotely, and I'm trying to ship the MVP by August. The team uses PostgreSQL 16 and I want to make sure migration is handled with Flyway from day one.
Got it — Berlin, remote, PostgreSQL 16, Flyway-driven migrations, August MVP. That gives us a clear picture to size the architecture around...
I chose Kotlin, Spring Boot 3.3, PostgreSQL 16, Ktor for the mesh, Flyway for migrations, and I plan to deploy via Docker Compose into Kubernetes on k3s when the MVP is stable.
Great decisions. To summarize your stack: Kotlin + Spring Boot 3.3, PostgreSQL 16 with Flyway, Ktor service mesh, Docker Compose -> k3s. That's a solid, modern path...
I work from a home office with a standing desk and I hate noisy coworking spaces. I always need a second monitor and I prefer mechanical keyboards, Cherry MX Browns specifically.
Standing desk, second monitor, mechanical keyboard with MX Browns — a very thoughtful setup. I'll remember those preferences when suggesting hardware or workspace configurations...
My goal is to spend 3 months a year working from abroad. I want a setup that works from a laptop on 4G, and I'm using Tailscale for the mesh and Obsidian for notes.
I use Arch Linux on the desktop, Ubuntu on the server, and I'm an Arch enthusiast who runs wayland with Hyprland.
We decided to stick with PostgreSQL instead of moving to a document store. The relational model plus JSONB gives us everything we need without adding a second datastore.
Solid reasoning. JSONB on PostgreSQL is often the pragmatic sweet spot — you keep referential integrity and still get document flexibility...
